title: Short Stuff: The Original Snake Oil Salesman
summary: Short Stuff episode tracing the origin of the term "snake oil." Josh and Chuck explain that original snake oil came from Chinese water snakes and was rich in omega-three fatty acids, used by Chinese immigrants (many working on the Transcontinental Railroad) for sore muscles and inflammation. Cowboy Clark Stanley turned it into a patent medicine in the 1890s, selling a liniment he claimed was made from rattlesnakes, sold with a pamphlet called The Life and Adventures of the American Cowboy. Stanley's product was actually beef fat, red pepper, mineral oil, camphor and turpentine, as tested in 1917. He was fined twenty dollars, and his fraud helped make "snake oil" a catch-all term for fake medicine and hustling. The hosts cite early uses of the phrase in Stephen Vincent Benét's poem John Brown's Body (1927) and Eugene O'Neill's The Iceman Cometh (1956). The episode references the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 from the previous day's episode.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the Short Stuff episode with light banter about Dave's absence and Chuck's throat tickle.

segments.title: Original snake oil from Chinese water snakes
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the topic of snake oil and patent medicines. Josh cites the Oxford English Dictionary definition of snake oil as a quack remedy. Chuck explains the original snake oil came from Chinese water snakes and was high in omega-three fatty acids, used for brain and heart health and inflammation.

segments.title: Chinese immigrants and the potent original remedy
segments.summary: Josh describes how the oil was used topically for sore muscles and inflammation and how nineteenth-century Chinese immigrants, many working on the Transcontinental Railroad, brought it to America. Chuck explains patent medicines and their secret ingredients, with sales at fifty cents a bottle.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode with a teaser for the next segment.

segments.title: Clark Stanley and the rattlesnake liniment
segments.summary: Clark Stanley, a cowboy turned patent medicine seller, claimed to make snake oil liniment from rattlesnakes and sold it with a pamphlet, The Life and Adventures of the American Cowboy. The label promised cures for many ailments. Josh notes rattlesnake oil is much less potent than the original Chinese water snake oil.
topics: The Life and Adventures of the American Cowboy

segments.title: Stanley's product exposed as fake
segments.summary: Chuck explains that Stanley did not use rattlesnake oil. Under the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906, his product was tested in 1917 and found to contain beef fat, red pepper, mineral oil, camphor and turpentine. He was fined twenty dollars.

segments.title: How snake oil became a term for fraud
segments.summary: Josh explains that Stanley's bust gave snake oil its bad reputation and made it a catch-all term for fake medicine and hustling. Chuck cites early uses in Stephen Vincent Benét's 1927 poem John Brown's Body and Eugene O'Neill's 1956 play The Iceman Cometh.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the episode and give the show credits.
